title: Little faith (Matthew 14:22–36)
hook: fine until you look at your feet: Peter on the water, warning or model?
tomorrow: can your hands be spotless while your heart isn't?

segments.voice: Yesterday, five loaves on the day John was buried, and compassion in grief. That same night, the disciples are out on the lake.

First time on a paddleboard, or on skates: you're steady until you look down at your feet. Then the wobble starts. Peter does exactly that, on water. It's night, the boat is tossed with waves, and a figure comes toward them walking on the sea. They cry out that it's a spirit. Then the voice: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." Peter answers: "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water." One word comes back: "Come."
screen: `STEADY UNTIL YOU LOOK DOWN.` → `IT IS I; BE NOT AFRAID.` → `COME.`

segments.voice: And Peter climbs out and walks. Then: "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" Christians read Peter here in two ways. Some hear a warning. Peter had the word come, and he took his eyes off the one who said it. The question, wherefore didst thou doubt, is a real rebuke, and the point is plain: keep looking at him, not at the wind. Others hear a model. The others stayed in the boat; one climbed out. He walked before he sank. When he went under, his prayer was three words long, and it worked. And look at the order: the hand comes first, immediately, and the question comes after, with Peter already held. On this reading, little faith is still faith, enough to get out of the boat. Both readings quote the same verses, and Matthew gives both a place. Then the wind stops, and those in the boat worship him: "Of a truth thou art the Son of God."
screen: `LORD, SAVE ME.` · `A WARNING: EYES OFF HIM, SINKING.` · `A MODEL: THE ONE WHO STEPPED OUT.` · `THE HAND FIRST, THE QUESTION AFTER.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand, fix your eyes on one point ahead of you, and take one slow step toward it. Feel the floor take your weight. Then stay there, still, and breathe, the way someone stands just after a step they weren't sure of.
Little faith. What Jesus calls Peter's faith on the water: small, wavering, and still enough to climb out of the boat.
Your line: reach out your hand. In Matthew, the hand comes before the question. Be well.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray Peter's three words, Lord, save me, in moments of fear, and some churches tell the story to children as a picture of keeping your eyes on Jesus.

fork.setup: a friend says: Peter is a cautionary tale, he doubted and sank. make the best case for the other reading.
options: Peter never really sank; the story is only a metaphor.
he alone stepped out, and the hand came first; little faith is still faith.
Jesus praised Peter's doubt as a kind of wisdom.
fork.reveal: the model reading quotes the text: Peter walked, cried Lord, save me, and immediately Jesus caught him before asking. the warning reading quotes the same verse: wherefore didst thou doubt?

original.note: Greek for O thou of little faith: one word in Matthew 14:31, little-faithed.

trapdoor: what you thought: little faith means no faith, a scolding.
what it means: a small, wavering faith, caught by a hand before it's questioned.
what a scholar hears: ὀλιγόπιστε, little-faithed, a word Matthew also uses in the storm of chapter 8; in both, the faith is small but not absent.
recall: new and old from one store
guess: small, wavering faith that's still faith
faith held by only a few in the crowd

chat.meaning: Jesus stretched forth his hand and caught Peter, then let him stand. Catching someone isn't taking their place.

notes: Debate shape: two Christian readings of Peter (a warning about looking away; a model of stepping out, with 'little faith' still faith) are both given their best case, quoting the same verses, with no denomination named and neither ranked. Confirm.
'The others stayed in the boat' avoids a head count (14:22 says only 'his disciples').
'His prayer was three words long' counts the KJV 'Lord, save me' (14:30). Confirm.
